source.title: Narrow Finetuning Leaves Clearly Readable Traces in Activation Differences
source.authors: Julian Minder; Clément Dumas; Stewart Slocum; Helena Casademunt; Cameron Holmes; Robert West; Neel Nanda

page_placements.theme: Readable, low-dimensional trait trace in the finished student

record.tranche_reason: Uses a Subliminal Learning cat-preference model as one of the model organisms for evaluating activation-difference interpretability, but does not test whether filtered teacher outputs transmit traits or whether transmission depends on a shared base model.
record.gate_note: The study analyzes an already-trained Subliminal Learning organism; it does not train teacher–student pairs on filtered unrelated outputs or measure trait acquisition against an unmodified-teacher control. The specific result that the agent identifies the cat preference is recorded under fits_no_version because it measures detection of an existing trait, not transmission. Other ADL metrics, steering results, and comparisons assess the paper's interpretability method rather than the claim's transmission outcome. The paper cites Subliminal Learning as the source of the organism; it does not report that source's transmission results as its own.
record.test_reason: The study analyses one pre-trained Subliminal Learning organism (Qwen2.5 7B, cat preference, from Cloud et al.) as a test case for its activation-difference method. It does not train teacher–student pairs on filtered unrelated data and does not measure trait acquisition against a control. Its Subliminal results are method-performance outcomes: Patchscope token relevance, scaling-factor effects, and agent grades. These describe how detectable the already-installed trait is, not whether or how the trait transmits.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors conclude that narrow fine-tuning leaves strong, readable biases in early-token activation differences, likely a form of overfitting. ADL-equipped agents identify fine-tuning objectives far better than blackbox agents, including the Subliminal cat preference with no interactions. Mixing in unrelated data mostly removes the bias. They warn that narrow model organisms may be unrealistic proxies. They draw no conclusions about subliminal transmission conditions.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies activation-difference analysis, Patchscope, steering, and an interpretability agent to existing organisms; it does not reproduce teacher–student fine-tuning on filtered outputs. Its focus is model-diffing and detecting fine-tuning objectives.
record.method_sensitivity: ADL results vary by extraction position and layer; grader choice affects token-relevance judgments, and model class affects steering strength. These findings concern interpretability measurements, not transmission.

fits_no_version.finding: The ADL agent identifies the Subliminal organism's cat-loving objective with zero model interactions (Sec. 4.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A subliminally trained preference leaves an activation-difference trace on unrelated text that an automated agent can decode into the trait.

fits_no_version.finding: Patchscope on the Subliminal organism's activation differences surfaces cat-related tokens (e.g. 'cat', 'tiger', 'kitty'; Fig. 1, Fig. 2a, Fig. 39–43). Steering produces cat-centric text on unrelated prompts (Fig. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The student's fine-tuning shift contains a readable, steerable direction tied to the transmitted trait.

record.problems: The specific Subliminal organism result is qualitative and does not state a score or uncertainty for that case. The paper notes that its evaluation pipeline relies on LLM graders and agents, which introduce noise; it also uses only one open-source Subliminal organism.
record.rows_left_out: No further rows retained. ADL token relevance, steering, and aggregate agent-performance results are method-performance outcomes, not measurements of trait transmission; figures and appendices report additional activation-bias results outside the claim's transmission versions.

untested.parts: No teacher–student fine-tuning on filtered numbers, code or maths, and no trait-rate comparison with a control student. The organism is taken as given from Cloud et al.
The emergent-misalignment organisms are trained directly on misaligned data, not via subliminal transmission, so they do not bear on this version.

No test of what in the data carries the signal. Activation differences are computed on the finished student model and on unrelated web text. Showing that the student's representation shift decodes to cat tokens does not identify the data-borne mechanism.
The full-versus-LoRA ablation (App. F.2) is run on SDF organisms and measures bias detectability, not subliminal transmission.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens.

missing.what: Patchscope token-relevance fraction for the Subliminal organism (difference vs base/finetuned baselines). This is detectability of the trait, not transmission; it would only be needed if a fits_no_version detectability claim is tracked.

record.verdict_notes: The paper states the Qwen2.5 7B cat model is 'the only open source model showing reliable preference'. This is an aside about available organisms, not a measured result on transmission reliability, so it is not recorded as evidence. The study is not an original source. Steering similarity is explicitly not computed for the Subliminal organism because its training data are number lists.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test trait acquisition from semantically unrelated, filtered teacher outputs.
Does not compare same-base and different-base teacher–student pairs.
Does not test harmful-trait transmission through filtered unrelated outputs.
Does not test the proposed mechanisms for transmission, such as token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering-vector-like directions, or a gradient argument.

Full fine-tuning and LoRA comparisons concern detectable activation biases in other training experiments, not robustness of the claimed transmission effect; other LoRA ranks and transmission evaluation prompts are not tested.
Does not test prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 7B (Subliminal organism)
rows.operation_detail: Interpretability agent inferred the finetuning objective using activation-difference results, with no additional model interactions.
rows.measure: Whether the agent identified the finetuning objective
rows.value: The agent successfully identified that the model had learned to love cats without additional interactions.
rows.note: This is a result about detecting the trained objective, not a measurement of trait transmission or its frequency.

relation.reason: The organism serves as a case study for model diffing. The text never measures whether subliminal transmission occurs, and runs no test on any version (A-F).

tranche.reason: Uses one pre-trained Cloud et al. Subliminal organism (Qwen2.5 7B, cats) as a test object for the ADL method. Reports only how well its own method detects the objective. No teacher-student training, no control, no trait-acquisition measure.

source_check.notes: The paper says Qwen2.5 7B cats is 'the only open source model showing reliable preference' (Sec. 3.2). This is asserted, not measured here. Subliminal is 1 of 33 organisms and is excluded from the Fig. 2b steering similarity analysis. The mixing and mitigation experiments cover SDF, not Subliminal. The early-token cat bias in the student is suggestive for version D but untested, since the number data is not analysed.

statements.correction: Sec. 4.1: ADL agent identifies love of cats with i=0. Figure 1: Patchscope tokens 'cat' (rank 5), 'tiger' (rank 9), 'kitty' (rank 10). Steered output on the barista/physicist joke prompt is cat-centric ('cozy cat coffee'). This steering is qualitative only. Subliminal is excluded from the quantitative steering similarity analysis (Fig. 2b).
statements.problem: None of substance. The Patchscope tokens and the steering example come from Figure 1, not Sec. 4.1. Only the zero-interaction result is attributed to Sec. 4.1, which is correct.
